Profuse

pruh-FYOOSS · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Profuse is exuberantly plentiful.

The gardener's rosebushes produced profuse blooms every June.

Worked Example

He offered profuse apologies to the entire staff after the scheduling error.

This wasn't a single quick apology -- it was an outpouring of many, many apologies, which is exactly profuse.

Your Turn

Answer correctly to continue.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

plentiful: Plentiful just says there is a lot of something — plentiful rain, plentiful jobs. Profuse goes further and adds a sense of pouring out: profuse apologies or profuse blossoms do not merely exist in quantity, they stream forth lavishly, almost more than the moment calls for.

generous: Generous describes a large amount that someone freely gives or grants — a generous tip, a generous helping. Profuse is about sheer outpouring: how lavishly something flows, streams, or grows on its own, with no giver involved at all.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

meager: small in amount and lacking in quantity

Where it sits · how far the supply goes beyond need — enough → profuse → overflowing

enough vs. profuse: Having enough means a need has been exactly met, with nothing extra; profuse goes far beyond need — an outpouring with plenty to spare.

overflowing vs. profuse: Profuse describes a lavish, abundant flow; overflowing means the supply has finally burst past what its container or space can hold.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — pro-

prefix — pro-: forth (Latin)

root — fuse

root — fuse: to pour (Latin (fundere))

Put it together

Put it together: Profuse comes from Latin pro- ('forth') + fundere ('to pour') -- literally 'poured forth,' describing something flowing out generously.

Use the root in a new word: refuse

Use the root in a new word: refuse: The same fundere root gives us refuse (re- 'back' + fundere, originally 'to pour back,' i.e. reject) and confuse (con- 'together' + fundere, 'to pour together').

Root Check

Word Choice

Profuse most often describes something flowing or growing plentifully -- sweat, apologies, blossoms, thanks -- always with a positive or at least mild, generous connotation.
